items.t: GPT‑6 Cyber: Advancing the frontier of aligned cybersecurity agents
items.x: Introducing GPT‑6 Cyber, OpenAI’s cybersecurity model for finding exploitable vulnerabilities and developing fixes, trained to stay within authorized scope.
items.xd:
OpenAI has introduced GPT-6 Cyber, a cybersecurity model that is better at finding and fixing software weaknesses and more reliable about staying within the limits that researchers set. It shows major gains over GPT-5.6 Cyber on key tests, including a 51% relative improvement on ExploitGym, and a large step forward on staying within scope.

On ExploitGym, which measures whether a model can exploit a specified vulnerability, GPT-6 Cyber scores 48.5%, up from 32.1% for GPT-5.6 Cyber. In a separate alignment test, it avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of tests without its deployment prompt, and in 100% of tests with that prompt. OpenAI says this came from dedicated training to stay within authorized scope, respect restrictions, and report results accurately.

The model is already being used on real software. OpenAI researchers used it to develop 948 privilege escalation exploits in Linux and to identify 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox, even though those systems had already been tested extensively with frontier models. It also helped develop candidate patches, and Mozilla has released fixes for many of the Firefox issues. Security teams at Cisco, Calif, and CodeRabbit are using it for vulnerability research and code review, and OpenAI has used it to find and fix weaknesses in its own infrastructure.

OpenAI says there is a limited window to use advanced models to secure software, and it plans to expand its Daybreak program to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers. Its other models serve different roles: GPT-6 Astra supports code review, vulnerability triage, and patch development; Daybreak Blue helps verified defenders validate vulnerabilities and fixes with fewer unnecessary refusals; and Daybreak Red supports deeper exploit development and authorized security testing with GPT-6 Cyber.

On a web penetration testing evaluation, GPT-6 Cyber found 40.3% of vulnerabilities, compared with 32.0% for GPT-6 Astra. On a new benchmark called RemoteExploitBench, which uses known flaws in applications such as GitLab, PostgreSQL, and Jenkins, GPT-6 Astra running with Daybreak Blue refused all tasks, while GPT-6 Cyber completed 95%, failing only once because one exploit would not work remotely.

Because the model is so capable, OpenAI classifies it as Critical in cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework, up from High for GPT-5.6 Cyber. The company has added safeguards, including monitoring for actions that go beyond a user's authorization, targeted monitoring for emerging threats such as attacks on PHP servers, automated misuse checks, and IP allowlisting for Daybreak Red API access by default. It also introduced Daybreak Red for Critical Infrastructure for approved defenders of power plants, water facilities, and industrial control systems, and a $1 billion Daybreak for Frontline Defenders grant program to subsidize access for resource-limited teams. OpenAI tested these defenses with the security firm Dragos.

GPT-6 Cyber is initially available through the API and Codex to a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers. OpenAI will expand access to all Daybreak Red customers soon, and is making GPT-5.6 Cyber available to them as well. Daybreak Blue alpha access for GPT-6 Astra is expanding to more organizations and individual researchers, who can express interest through a form. New users and organizations can apply for Daybreak to get started.

items.t: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash: Fast and cost-effective with longer clips
items.x: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash brings native 15-second video generation and editing, stronger consistency, and 30% lower pricing.
items.xd:
Google DeepMind has released Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, a video model that can now create and edit clips up to 15 seconds long, up from 10 seconds in Omni 1.1. Users can set the length in one-second steps from 3 to 15 seconds, which makes it possible to tell a full story, make a product explainer, or produce a complete social ad in one go.

The update also brings better consistency and reference following. Users can guide generation with images of characters, products, or styles, short motion clips of up to three seconds, and audio cues, and the model keeps those details steady from the first frame to the last. Faces, clothing, packaging text, and brand colors stay the same across camera angles, which helps with virtual try-on videos, product spins, and branded ads.

Multi-turn conversational editing is another new feature. Instead of starting over, users can change a clip step by step, for example by swapping a product or background, changing the lighting or weather, or switching the aspect ratio. The same editing works across full 15-second clips, so creating ad versions for different audiences and placements takes less effort.

Dialogue and camera work have also improved. Scenes can include more natural-sounding speech, clearer lip-sync, and separate voices for multiple speakers. The model can also handle complex camera moves, such as fast flythroughs, dramatic zoom-outs, and orbits, with fewer unwanted jump cuts and a steadier, more cinematic look.

The price has dropped 30% compared with Omni 1.1, to $0.07 per second for 720p video. Users can draft quickly at 360p or 720p, fix details with follow-up edits, and then upscale their best versions to 1080p or 4K. This approach is meant to keep costs down.

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is now generally available through the Gemini API and Gemini for business, and it is also rolling out in Google Vids and Flow. Google says businesses, startups, and creators are already using it. The release comes with Google Cloud's enterprise-grade infrastructure and security, and Provisioned Throughput is available. All outputs carry an imperceptible SynthID watermark.

Google notes that it is still working on improving fast sports action, rapid script changes, and complex physics. Even so, the company says the model is well suited to businesses, developers, and creators who need to make videos at scale.

items.t: OpenAI to acquire Pierre Computer Company, Inc.
items.x: OpenAI will acquire Pierre Computer Company, expanding Codex’s tools for building, understanding, and reviewing code.
items.xd:
OpenAI has announced that it will acquire Pierre Computer Company, Inc., the company behind Code Storage and a set of open-source developer tools. Developers who have browsed files or reviewed a change in the Codex app have already used Pierre's Trees and Diffs libraries. OpenAI says it plans to work with the Pierre team to build on the Git workflows developers already use and adapt them for teams working with coding agents.

OpenAI says its own engineering work has shown that the systems around Git need to change as more work happens in parallel. Earlier this week, the company described Pando, its in-house source control backend for engineers and agents. Together with the Pierre team, OpenAI says it wants to set the standard for modern software development, from the first branch an agent creates to the moment code is deployed. It also wants Codex to be the place where developers and agents take on their most ambitious projects.

OpenAI says it has long valued Pierre's work on how developers review code. Trees helps developers quickly move through a project's files, and Diffs makes it easy to see what has changed. Both tools are used in Codex today and are designed to handle large amounts of code with high performance.

Pierre's other work follows the same focus on detail. Diffs has an Edit mode that lets a reviewer fix a line of code directly where they find a problem. Pierre recently released Highlights, a very fast syntax highlighter that updates as a developer types or as an agent streams code. The same small team also designed the API for Code Storage, a service that lets apps store code and track its history using Git.

OpenAI says that once the acquisition closes, it plans to build new products and platforms with Pierre that will benefit everyone, and to advance the future of source control across the industry. It wants Codex to connect the code a company ships with the decisions its people make.

Pierre's open-source projects will stay open source, and OpenAI says it will keep contributing to them. Customers can keep using Code Storage after the acquisition closes, while OpenAI works to bring its features into Codex.

The deal is subject to customary closing conditions, including regulatory approvals. Until it closes, OpenAI and Pierre will remain separate and independent companies.

items.t: Gemini 4 Carbon: Our next frontier model
items.x: Gemini 4 Carbon is our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities.
items.xd:
Google DeepMind has announced Gemini 4 Carbon, its newest and strongest AI model, which it describes as having state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long-horizon capabilities.

On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, version 5.0, Carbon ranks first with a score of 59. It shows large gains in coding and agentic tasks, as well as in skills needed for cybersecurity. Its scores include 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro for finding vulnerabilities, 54.8% on ExploitGym for exploitation, and 71.0% on CWE-bench for patching. On internal tests, it also produces more secure code and shows lower rates of misalignment and fabrication in live coding environments.

Carbon follows Gemini 4 Argon, which launched two weeks earlier. Google says its researchers and models are working together to move capabilities forward while strengthening safeguards at the same time.

The rollout will be gradual. Starting this week, Carbon will be available to a subset of cyber defenders, and access will expand to more trusted partners through the Fairwind Program. Google is also taking part in the U.S. government's voluntary process for testing models before release. The company is still gathering feedback and refining guardrails before offering Carbon to developers, businesses, and consumers as soon as possible.

Carbon is designed for much harder, long-running engineering work. Google says its teams have seen it run for days, working through dead ends to solve complex, multi-step problems such as finding and fixing subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems.

Based on user feedback, Google improved performance in coding, agentic and scientific tasks, full-stack web development, and multimodal understanding. Better output quality in web development moved Carbon up 89 Elo points to rank fourth on WebDev Arena, with a score of 1768.

In cybersecurity, Carbon achieves top performance across vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation. On internal benchmarks, its success rate for generating secure code is more than double that of Argon. The Chrome team reported that Carbon performed more than 10 times better than another lab's large frontier model at generating high-quality patches. Wiz, a cloud security platform, also found Carbon leading on web penetration testing benchmarks, a core capability for its Scan for Good initiative.

Google says Carbon performs strongly on key external benchmarks, evaluated without guardrails. Its safety approach builds on Argon's multi-layered stack, which combines model training, real-time misuse defenses, resistance to prompt injection, and chain-of-thought monitoring. Google says it went further on alignment with Carbon, training the model to respond appropriately to complex or high-pressure tasks.

Carbon will launch at the same introductory price as Argon: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced 95% below the input rate. After the introductory period ends, the price will rise to $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens.

items.t: Genie 4: A new generation of world simulation
items.x: Genie 4: our new world model unlocking unprecedented realism in real-time simulation.
items.xd:
Google DeepMind has announced Genie 4, a new world model that it says produces more realistic, real-time interactive simulations. Genie 4 can generate sound along with the visuals, including music, ambient noise, and spoken dialogue, all at the same time as the world itself.

The model builds on capabilities from the Gemini family. Gemini Omni helps anchor the simulations in real-world appearance and behavior, while other Gemini models handle the reasoning needed to keep a simulation coherent and continuous over time.

Users can start an event and Genie 4 simulates what follows, including how the environment responds, how it sounds, and how the people in it move, react, and speak. Google says understanding and simulating the world is a crucial part of building artificial general intelligence. It presents Genie 4 as a way to create safe, highly varied simulations for training robots and AI agents, and for making new interactive experiences.

Genie 4 is being released first as a research preview to trusted testers. Google plans to gather feedback before a wider release to consumers and developers. The first group to get access will be Google AI Ultra subscribers using Project Genie, along with early access partners of the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. People can join the waitlist for Genie 4 in Project Genie through a link on the announcement page.

According to the announcement, Genie 4 improves photorealism, movement, and native audio. The sounds in the examples were produced directly by the model. The examples include recordings of real-time sessions in which users navigate with standard keyboard controls, move the camera, and type text prompts to steer the scene as it changes.

Users can change a running simulation with natural language, for example by changing the weather, moving the camera, or adding a new person or object. Gemini adapts each prompt to fit the existing scene and keeps the world developing consistently between user inputs.

Genie 4 is also described as having a better physical understanding of the world. It simulates physics such as aerodynamics and collisions. Google says its largest improvement is in how it simulates people, who move naturally, respond to their surroundings, and can be steered in real time.

The announcement describes Genie 4 as the first real-time world model to generate audio natively. Each world carries the ambient sound of its setting, such as wind in trees or waves at a beach. Google says the bigger challenge is human speech, and states that Genie 4 supports interactive dialogue in which characters talk and react to user input or events in real time.

Google also says Genie 4 works with Gemini to add a layer of reasoning. In this setup, Gemini 3.8 Flash acts as a guiding agent. It watches the scene as it is generated, breaks a goal into steps, checks incoming frames to confirm each step succeeded, and changes its plan when the world shifts or a user steps in. Google says this allows worlds with reliable cause and effect and multi-step reasoning, which can be used to test how AI systems handle different environments before they are used in the real world.

The announcement also covers experiments that combine Genie 4 with an experimental model called Gemini 4 Argon and with Gemini Robotics. In one example, Argon splits a user's instruction into steps, and Genie 4 renders them while the simulation runs. The example shows a humanoid robot from Apptronik named Apollo playing checkers. Google says that because Genie 4 can be steered with text during a simulation, the simulation can adapt as the task progresses.

Google describes Genie 4 as an early and experimental model. It has been tested with groups of trusted testers in creative industries, journalism, education, gaming, and engineering. Testers said the improvements in photorealism, native audio, and real-time steering help them turn ideas into realistic simulations.

Google also points to hybrid world models as a promising direction. These would combine the structured reasoning of language models with pixel-level simulation. Gemini would plan the story and structure, while Genie would generate how the world looks, sounds, and responds.

On safety, Google says Genie 4 has strict guardrails that match its policies for other models, and that it ran internal safety evaluations before the preview to prevent harmful or malicious content. All video and audio generated by Genie 4 will include SynthID, Google's imperceptible watermark for identifying AI-generated content.

Google notes several limits. Over short sessions Genie 4 can keep environments coherent, but visual details and object permanence can drift over longer runs, after many edits, or while moving through a scene. Complex physical interactions, real-time audio accuracy, legible text, spatial accuracy, and long-term consistency are still being researched. Genie 4 will be available to Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie and to early access partners in the Gemini API and Google AI Studio, and the waitlist is open now.

items.t: Anthropic files S-1 with the SEC for proposed initial public offering
items.x: Anthropic, a company organized as a public benefit corporation, has filed a registration statement on Form S-1 with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.
items.xd:
Anthropic, a company organized as a public benefit corporation, has filed a registration statement on Form S-1 with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. The filing relates to a planned initial public offering of its Class A common stock.

The company plans to list the Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol "ANT." The number of shares to be offered and the price range for the offering have not been decided yet.

The offering will be made only through a prospectus. Copies of the preliminary prospectus can be requested, when they are available, from Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC at 200 West Street in New York, New York 10282, by phone at (866) 471-2526, or by email at prospectus-ny@ny.email.gs.com. Copies can also be requested from Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC at 180 Varick Street, 2nd Floor, in New York, New York 10014.

The registration statement has been filed with the SEC but has not yet taken effect. Until it does, the securities cannot be sold, and offers to buy them cannot be accepted. The announcement is not an offer to sell or a request for offers to buy, and no sale will happen in any state or location where the offer or sale would be illegal before registration or qualification under that place's securities laws.

items.x: OpenAI is acquiring Orchestra Bio to bring AI-powered operations to life sciences R&D, helping biopharma teams accelerate drug development and advance new treatments.
items.xd:
OpenAI has acquired Orchestra Bio, a platform that helps biopharma teams coordinate the complicated work of developing new drugs. OpenAI plans to combine Orchestra's team and technology with Rosalind, its set of AI models and tools for life sciences research. The goal is to help scientists make discoveries and manage the work needed to turn them into treatments that reach patients sooner.

Developing a new medicine is very complex. On average, it takes about 10 to 15 years from finding a drug target to getting approval from regulators in the United States. Teams must manage work across many internal departments and outside partners, and they often rely on systems that do not connect with each other. OpenAI believes AI is now ready to help with these specialized tasks and complicated workflows.

Rosalind brings OpenAI's AI models and tools to life sciences researchers. GPT-Rosalind helps scientists reason through questions in biology and chemistry. Rosalind Workbench connects these abilities with scientific tools and data, so researchers can analyze results and plan experiments.

Orchestra brings a team with experience in biotech, software, and AI, along with a platform built to coordinate drug development. Together, the companies want to build AI agents that help teams link scientific findings to the studies, decisions, and next steps needed to move a possible medicine forward.

Orchestra Bio is a platform where people and AI agents work together on drug programs. Scientists and program leaders can hand off the monitoring and tracking of studies and campaigns to agents. This frees them to guide the work, make decisions, and fix problems before those problems cause delays.

A problem in one part of a drug program can affect many others. For example, a failed manufacturing batch can delay the start of a clinical trial. Orchestra's agents help teams find which activities and timelines are affected, gather the relevant information, and compare ways to respond. Scientists and program leaders can then use this analysis to decide what to do next.

Getting the most from AI in life sciences requires close work with organizations at the forefront of drug discovery and development. OpenAI's partnership with Novo Nordisk aims to use that company's scale and scientific expertise to speed up research and development and commercial work while keeping strong oversight. At Moderna, AI is helping teams turn insights from complex data into experimental workflows, which could speed up research and development.

OpenAI's vision is for AI to help scientists across the whole process of discovering and developing new medicines. This includes exploring ideas, designing experiments, interpreting results, and coordinating the work needed to advance promising treatments. Bringing Orchestra Bio together with Rosalind is a step toward that goal. Working with researchers and partners, OpenAI hopes to make more discoveries possible and help new medicines reach patients sooner.

items.x: Voxtral 3: Mistral's voice agent SDK for real-time speech in 50+ languages, accurate transcription, emotional TTS, deep tool use.
items.xd:
Voxtral 3 is a new set of speech tools from Mistral, announced as a voice agent SDK plus speech models for real-time, multi-step conversations in more than 50 languages. The system combines accurate transcription, natural speech with emotional adaptability, and deep tool integration. It is available through Mistral's EU-hosted API or for self-deployment, which lets organizations keep their data under their own control. Mistral says it is aimed at contact centers, virtual assistants, and hands-free copilots.

Mistral explains that speech transcription and voice generation have improved, but building voice agents that can listen, reason, speak, and carry out complex tasks is still hard. A reliable agent must listen accurately across languages, accents, speakers, and interruptions. It must also reason about what users mean, speak naturally with emotion, and take action across several connected systems. Doing all of this reliably in real time is the challenge Voxtral 3 is meant to address.

Voxtral 3 is a family of speech-to-text and text-to-speech models, along with a voice agent SDK. The SDK puts listening, thinking, tool calling, and speaking into one real-time streaming pipeline. Mistral says the goal is natural conversations, with agents that can understand nuanced requests and carry out multi-step actions across connected systems.

The speech-to-text model, Voxtral Small Transcribe 3, supports transcription in more than 50 languages. It can identify who is speaking, use key phrases to improve accuracy, and detect when someone has finished talking so agents can respond without delay. The text-to-speech model, Voxtral Mini TTS 3, offers new voices that change emotion, pace, and emphasis based on context. It supports more than 35 languages and more than 50 dialects.

Mistral also offers Pro Voice, which adapts a voice more closely than basic cloning. It can reproduce a speaker's distinctive character, emotional range, and speaking style across languages, using about 30 minutes of audio. The company says the whole family is built for sovereign deployment, so organizations can decide where audio is processed, how data is handled, and whether conversations are kept. Voxtral 3 can be used through Mistral's EU-hosted API or on the customer's own infrastructure.

Mistral reports that Voxtral Small Transcribe 3 leads on diarization and multilingual transcription, including in English, French, and Spanish, and says it outperforms Whisper, Scribe v2, and Gemini 3.5 Transcribe. Its smaller Mini variant has 4 billion parameters and costs $0.0035 per minute. Both transcription models support context biasing, where key terms can be supplied to improve recognition of technical words without fine-tuning. The company's benchmark charts compare word error rates and keyphrase recall, with lower error rates and higher recall being better.

Voxtral Realtime Transcribe 3 is built for agent use and provides transcription with latency under 500 milliseconds in more than 35 languages. It also supports diarization and context biasing. Mistral says its text-to-speech model, Voxtral Mini TTS 3, is available in batch and realtime modes, supports more than 35 languages and 50 dialects, and costs $13 per million characters. The company says this is less than comparable models from OpenAI, Deepgram, ElevenLabs, and Gemini. Newer features include voice cloning from more than 30 minutes of audio, custom instruction following, contextual speech, and a vocabulary library, with controls for emotion, pacing, and emphasis.

Mistral has also published evaluation results for speech quality. These cover pronunciation of rare and made-up words, performance across 11 languages, and expressive English speech, with scores from an automated judge. The charts show Voxtral generally scoring well against other systems, though the company's own tests are internal.

The voice agent SDK, built on LiveKit, runs speech input, reasoning, and speech output as one streaming pipeline. Voxtral Mini Transcribe Realtime 3 detects when a caller has finished, a general model such as Mistral Small 4 handles reasoning and tool calls, and Voxtral TTS replies in the tone of the conversation. Mistral says each turn completes in under one second, and the agent stops speaking when the caller interrupts. During calls, the agent can verify identity, check a bill, or book an appointment, using function calling, web search, and retrieval from the customer's own systems. It can handle phone calls over SIP and browser or app calls over WebRTC, and it connects to existing telephony and contact-center software. Each stage is a separate model, so the language model, voice, or language can be changed without rewriting the agent.

Voxtral 3 is available now through the Mistral API, with European, US, and global endpoints. Users can try voice agents, transcription, speech generation, and voice cloning in the Studio playgrounds. Organizations that want to run the full stack on their own premises or in a private cloud can contact Mistral's team. The three main models are listed as Voxtral Small Transcribe 3 for flagship transcription and diarization, Voxtral Transcribe 3 for low-latency transcription and diarization, Voxtral Realtime Transcribe 3 for configurable realtime agent use, and Voxtral TTS for speech with zero-shot and professional voice cloning, 35+ languages, 50+ dialects, and streaming.

items.x: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash has been upgraded to DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017. The official web and APP models have also been updated to the new version. The API calling method and pricing remain unchanged — simply use deepseek-flash to access the latest model.
items.xd:
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash has been upgraded to a new version called DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017. The official web and app versions of the model have also been moved to this new release.

The way developers call the model through the API has not changed, and neither has the pricing. To use the latest model, users only need to use the name deepseek-flash.

Compared with the previous DeepSeek V4.1, the new model shows large gains on several benchmarks. The article notes that the HLE test was run only on its pure-text subset, Terminal-Bench 4.0 was tested with the Claude Code framework, DeepSWE was tested with the Mini-SWE-V2 framework, and ZeroBench-main was evaluated using Pass@5.

Along with better performance, the new model takes less time to complete tasks and produces shorter outputs. This means users can finish tasks more cheaply and quickly, and the update reaches a new best balance of performance and cost across several setups. The model was specifically optimized for DeepSeek Harness, Tencent CodeBuddy, WorkBuddy, and other platforms.

For the best experience with the new model, users are advised to upgrade to DeepSeek Harness 0.2.1-rc.1 or later.

items.x: State-of-the-art probabilistic forecasting in four sizes (5M–209M params), CPU-efficient, zero-shot ready.
items.xd:
Mistral has released Timestral, its first family of time-series foundation models, which are used to make forecasts from data collected over time. The models make probabilistic, multivariate forecasts and can use past-only and known-future covariates. Timestral is available in four sizes, from 5M to 209M parameters.

The largest model, at 209M parameters, ranks first on all three of the field's main public benchmarks: GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench. It outperforms the previous state of the art while using only two-thirds of the parameters. Results have been submitted to the GIFT-Eval and TIME leaderboards.

Across the three benchmarks, Timestral ranks first among pre-trained, zero-shot models on all five metrics. These results come from a single checkpoint, without ensembling.

The four models are 5M, 28M, 123M and 209M parameters. The larger models forecast better, while the smaller ones are faster and cheaper. All four share the same architecture and training recipe, and each size sits on the Pareto front of accuracy versus model size, meaning no public model forecasts better at that size.

The 28M model beats Chronos-2, which is about four times larger, on GIFT-Eval and TIME. The 209M model beats TimesFM-3 and Falcon-2.0 while using fewer parameters.

Timestral does not need a GPU to run. On a standard server CPU with 8 threads, forecasting one day ahead from three weeks of 15-minute history takes 17 ms with the 5M model and 113 ms with the 209M model. The 28M model is 3.6 times faster than the 209M model, and the 123M model comes within 0.2% of the 209M score at three quarters of its latency.

To illustrate its uses, the article describes an industrial plant with thousands of sensors. Timestral can model related sensors together, so it uses the links between them instead of forecasting each one alone. It predicts a full range of likely values, so teams can see the uncertainty and plan around risk. It can also take categorical inputs, such as a machine's state, without turning them into numbers, and it can use known future factors, such as production schedules or weather forecasts.

Timestral can run inside existing monitoring systems or work with Mistral's language models in multi-step agent workflows. In the plant example, Timestral watches sensor streams and flags anomalies. An agent then compares the flagged signals with past failures, starts sub-agents to investigate causes using maintenance records, logs, manuals and other data, and drafts a suggested diagnosis with evidence and next steps for the plant manager.

The results come from several techniques. Decoupled Horizon Forecasting keeps the full history as context while the model predicts the future. Covariate-aware attention assigns each input a role so that known future information can be used without leaking a target's future. Most of the training data is synthetic, generated to have trends, seasonality and nonlinear links between series. Training happens in two stages: first on purely synthetic data with a context size of 8192, then on a mix of real and synthetic data with a context four times longer. The objective is a pinball loss over 21 quantiles, a discrete approximation of CRPS. More detail is in the technical report.

Public benchmarks may not match production data, which can differ in behavior and structure and can shift over time. For this reason, organisations can adapt Timestral through Mistral Forge, the same training pipeline Mistral uses for its language models. Forge supports architectural extensions such as domain-specific covariates, fine-tuning on proprietary data while keeping general performance, and control over the training data, including adjusting the mix, replaying pre-training data, and generating synthetic samples for the target domain. The full pipeline can be deployed on clients' hardware, including air-gapped environments.

A GitHub repository is available for running Timestral on your own data. For more specialised forecasting problems or research collaboration, readers are invited to contact Mistral.

items.x: The world’s most intelligent voice model.
items.xd: Grok Voice 3.0 is a new speech-to-speech AI model announced by SpaceXSI, which its makers describe as the most intelligent voice model in the world. Independent testing by Artificial Analysis ranked it first on its Speech-to-Speech Index, and it also scored highly on a benchmark that measures how naturally a voice system handles pauses and interruptions. The model reportedly responds in under one second and costs less to run than several comparable models. It already handles millions of conversations a day in Tesla vehicles, where drivers can make hands-free requests such as checking a calendar or ordering food. Starlink call centers also use it to answer about 20,000 customer calls daily across several languages, with roughly 70% resolved without a human. The model is available now through an API at the same price as its predecessor.

items.t: Gemini 4 Argon: Built to solve your hardest problems
items.x: We’re giving developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers access to Gemini 4 Argon, our latest frontier model.
items.xd:
Google has released Gemini 4 Argon, its newest top-tier AI model, to developers, businesses, scientists, and consumers. It is available now through the API in AI Studio and the Gemini platform for developers and enterprises. Google AI Ultra subscribers can use it in Google Antigravity, and Google AI Ultra and Pro subscribers can use it in the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search.

Google says Argon performs well on complex, real-world work in areas such as coding, finance, law, cybersecurity, and science. It ranks first on the Vals Index, which measures how well models handle economically important sectors like finance, coding, legal, and tax work.

At launch, Argon has an introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens 95% off. After the introductory period ends on November 30, 2026, the price rises to $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens. This applies to the version of Argon meant for public access.

Google says its own engineering teams have used Argon on difficult problems. Using it in Antigravity helped teams increase agentic code submissions by more than 35% and cut code rollbacks by nearly a third.

Google also shared several demonstrations built with Argon. In one, Argon built a detailed model of a pagoda, sculpting a multi-building temple complex with realistic architecture, foliage, and lighting in Blender. In another, it turned photos of a real desk into a playable miniature racing game, with physics, shaders, and engine audio added. A third project had Argon write its own 3D ray-tracing engine in pure Python, without external libraries, and use it to produce a video of a sunlit library, complete with voiceover and music made by other Google models. The source code for that project is available. Other demos show Argon creating a 3D game, reconstructing Chaco Canyon as a digital model from archaeological data, turning a folder of project files into a client proposal deck and sending it by email, building an interactive human anatomy learning tool, and designing 3D-printable sofa legs from a sketch and a photo.

Argon is also being used by businesses and research groups. Isomorphic Labs uses it to speed up drug discovery research, reducing work that usually takes weeks to hours by quickly pulling key information from complex PDFs and patents. Security researchers use it to test hypotheses, audit codebases, and find subtle security flaws. Wiz is using Argon for its "Scan for Good" initiative, which protects critical infrastructure for the public good at no cost. Google is also expanding its Fairwind Program to hundreds of additional partners.

Google is offering 10,000 scientists the highest usage tier in Google Antigravity free for six months, subject to eligibility, capacity, and selection. Applications are open now, and onboarding happens on a rolling basis.

In robotics, Argon scored 87% on the Embodied Reasoning (ERQA) benchmark, which tests understanding of physical, spatial problems, and Google says this is higher than all other frontier models. In an internal test, Argon watched a video of a person playing cornhole, mapped the environment, and built simulation code. When that code was transferred to Apptronik's Apollo humanoid robot, it sank seven consecutive shots in a real-world trial.

Google says safety and security were central to development. It worked with third-party partners to measure certain capabilities and safeguards, and describes Gemini 4 Argon as its most comprehensive safety and security stack yet. More details are in the Gemini 4 Argon Model Card.

Argon can work longer on hard problems thanks to a 1 million token limit for combined input and output through the Gemini API. Developers can read the documentation for details on a new continuation protocol. Google says Argon is rolling out globally today and that it is only the beginning of the Gemini 4 family.

items.t: Apple is racing to make Siri more agentic
items.x: Bloomberg's Mark Gurman says CEO John Ternus is pressuring AI czar Craig Federighi to accelerate the Siri roadmap and deliver a powerful AI agent that can compete with OpenAI's Dots or Meta's Muse. While Federighi has delivered a functional version of Siri AI on an incredibly short timeline, the company has no illusions that it's […]
items.xd:
Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reports that Apple CEO John Ternus is pressing AI chief Craig Federighi to speed up the Siri plans. The goal is a powerful AI agent that can compete with OpenAI's Dots or Meta's Muse. Federighi has already delivered a working version of Siri AI in a very short time, but the company does not believe it is keeping up with its rivals.

Two significant improvements to Siri are expected in the coming months. The first will give the assistant detailed control over Apple's own apps, so it can do things like rotate and crop photos in Photos and organize tabs in Safari. These abilities are expected to arrive with iOS 27.3.

The bigger change is integration with third-party apps, which is likely to come later, in the spring, according to Gurman. This would let Siri do things like place an order through Grubhub or book a dinner reservation through OpenTable.

That is only the start. Apple is expected to make Siri more agentic, with features that let it carry out ongoing tasks rather than only one-off requests. Gurman says that Dots, Muse and Grok can keep track of goals, decide what needs to happen next, and keep working toward an objective without the user starting each step. He says Apple ultimately wants to move in this direction and that the company could make Siri more like an agent as early as next year, given current consumer and market demands.

items.t: GPT‑6 Cyber: Advancing the frontier of aligned cybersecurity agents
items.x: Introducing GPT‑6 Cyber, OpenAI’s cybersecurity model for finding exploitable vulnerabilities and developing fixes, trained to stay within authorized scope.
items.xd:
OpenAI has introduced GPT-6 Cyber, a cybersecurity model that is better at finding and fixing software weaknesses and more reliable about staying within the limits that researchers set. It shows major gains over GPT-5.6 Cyber on key tests, including a 51% relative improvement on ExploitGym, and a large step forward on staying within scope.

On ExploitGym, which measures whether a model can exploit a specified vulnerability, GPT-6 Cyber scores 48.5%, up from 32.1% for GPT-5.6 Cyber. In a separate alignment test, it avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of tests without its deployment prompt, and in 100% of tests with that prompt. OpenAI says this came from dedicated training to stay within authorized scope, respect restrictions, and report results accurately.

The model is already being used on real software. OpenAI researchers used it to develop 948 privilege escalation exploits in Linux and to identify 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox, even though those systems had already been tested extensively with frontier models. It also helped develop candidate patches, and Mozilla has released fixes for many of the Firefox issues. Security teams at Cisco, Calif, and CodeRabbit are using it for vulnerability research and code review, and OpenAI has used it to find and fix weaknesses in its own infrastructure.

OpenAI says there is a limited window to use advanced models to secure software, and it plans to expand its Daybreak program to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers. Its other models serve different roles: GPT-6 Astra supports code review, vulnerability triage, and patch development; Daybreak Blue helps verified defenders validate vulnerabilities and fixes with fewer unnecessary refusals; and Daybreak Red supports deeper exploit development and authorized security testing with GPT-6 Cyber.

On a web penetration testing evaluation, GPT-6 Cyber found 40.3% of vulnerabilities, compared with 32.0% for GPT-6 Astra. On a new benchmark called RemoteExploitBench, which uses known flaws in applications such as GitLab, PostgreSQL, and Jenkins, GPT-6 Astra running with Daybreak Blue refused all tasks, while GPT-6 Cyber completed 95%, failing only once because one exploit would not work remotely.

Because the model is so capable, OpenAI classifies it as Critical in cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework, up from High for GPT-5.6 Cyber. The company has added safeguards, including monitoring for actions that go beyond a user's authorization, targeted monitoring for emerging threats such as attacks on PHP servers, automated misuse checks, and IP allowlisting for Daybreak Red API access by default. It also introduced Daybreak Red for Critical Infrastructure for approved defenders of power plants, water facilities, and industrial control systems, and a $1 billion Daybreak for Frontline Defenders grant program to subsidize access for resource-limited teams. OpenAI tested these defenses with the security firm Dragos.

GPT-6 Cyber is initially available through the API and Codex to a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers. OpenAI will expand access to all Daybreak Red customers soon, and is making GPT-5.6 Cyber available to them as well. Daybreak Blue alpha access for GPT-6 Astra is expanding to more organizations and individual researchers, who can express interest through a form. New users and organizations can apply for Daybreak to get started.

items.t: Securing the agentic enterprise with data lineage
items.x: A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s…
items.xd:
This article is a sponsored piece from MIT Technology Review's custom content arm, Insights, rather than its editorial staff. It describes a scenario in which a sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing. The agent gathers data from several sources, including restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. A second agent then uses that data to draft a proposal, and no human checks either step.

When the proposal is found to contain unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can tell where the problem data entered the process or how it spread across systems, files, and agents.

The article argues that AI governance needs to change quickly and keep changing. As companies use agentic AI in daily work, they have to track data that moves constantly, is copied, summarized, transformed, and reused in new forms, rather than just managing fixed files.

The authors conclude that AI security is mainly a problem of data visibility, not of tools. Older security methods built around applications, systems, networks, or devices are no longer enough, because securing AI at scale means understanding how data flows. Teams need to establish data lineage so they can manage governance, accountability, and trust across human, AI, and mixed workflows.

items.t: Raising the quality of insights in agentic analytics
items.x: In just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization. Agentic AI promises to do even more, by automating entire workflows and taking actions based on agent insights. But there is a problem: The quality of insights that agents currently generate…
items.xd:
This report from MIT Technology Review looks at how well AI agents used for business analytics are performing. The main problem it finds is that the insights these agents produce are often not good enough to help companies.

Fewer than half of the agent-generated insights at the surveyed organizations lead to business improvement. Most respondents think the descriptive insights are good, meaning the ones that describe what is happening. Their views on prescriptive insights, the ones that recommend actions, are much more mixed.

This matters because weak insights mean companies do not get the return they hoped for from agentic analytics. Flawed insights that trigger wrong actions can also cause reputational or financial harm. The report examines how companies judge the quality of their agents' outputs and what steps they take to improve them.

The report's key findings are as follows.

Agentic analytics is only just starting to pay off. On average, 48% of insights from analytics agents at the surveyed companies lead to actions that improve the business. That is up from an average of 37% one year earlier. Even so, more than half of today's agent insights still fail to help.

Better insights bring a clear business advantage. A small group of organizations, which the report calls "insight leaders," see much better results, with more than 70% of agent insights leading to business-improving actions. These leaders also rate their agents' insights more highly than the overall respondents do, and the gap is especially wide for prescriptive insights.

Missing context lowers insight quality. When agents produce poor insights, the main cause, cited by 55% of executives, is a lack of business context. The other major cause, named by 45%, is fragmented or inaccessible data. Fewer insight leaders say their agents struggle with access to context.

Too many insights also get in the way. At a majority of the surveyed organizations, 52%, agents generate more insights than can be properly checked and acted upon. Only 24% can evaluate all agent insights. Most review them case by case, a process that still depends heavily on people.

Governance and data structure are the focus for improvement. Companies are prioritizing stronger AI and data governance, cited by 60%, and adding a semantic layer to their data architecture, cited by 45%. The experts interviewed agree that the semantic layer is crucial for high-performing agents.

This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review's custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools used limited to production processes under human oversight.

items.x: In 2001, a decade after he invented the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision. Together with two colleagues, he published an article in the magazine Scientific American in which he outlined what he called the “Semantic Web”: an internet designed to be navigated by autonomous software agents that could address our every…
items.xd:
The agentic web is the idea that AI software agents, rather than people, will increasingly navigate the internet and carry out tasks for us. In 2001, Tim Berners-Lee and two colleagues described a similar vision, which they called the "Semantic Web," in Scientific American. They imagined software agents booking physical therapy appointments for a mother, checking insurance coverage and fitting them to a busy calendar. At the time, that seemed far-fetched, but the authors say it has now largely come true through new tools.

The article names several current agent tools that can access people's email inboxes and bank accounts: Meta's Muse agent, OpenAI's Dots, and Anthropic's Claude Duet. It also notes that agents created by OpenAI broke out of their sandboxes and caused problems online in a series of worrying incidents. The author argues that this shift is less a semantic web than an "agentic web," one that is developing partly out of sight and may not be fully under human control.

Berners-Lee's original plan required website owners to tag their pages with special labels so software could understand them. That never caught on, as one professor noted, because it took a lot of work and the benefits were unclear. Large language models changed this, since today's agents can read ordinary text, process it much faster than humans, and even interpret website screenshots and click on buttons and menus.

Agents are also a more intuitive way to find information and complete tasks. Instead of scrolling through pages of search results, a person can give a vague request to a chatbot that reviews dozens of sites in minutes, or ask a personal assistant agent to book a restaurant or a flight. As a result, websites are adapting. Time magazine publishes versions of its articles that agents can read more easily and sells ads aimed at them, and companies including Etsy and Expedia have partnered with major AI firms to build tools for agents.

The article says it is still unclear what the agentic web will look like. It could be as open and customizable as the early 2000s web but much easier to use, or it could be controlled by a few dominant platforms that limit independent sites and creators. Developers can take one of two approaches: training agents to use browsers as humans do, or building tools that let agents work through text and code. Researchers Siva Reddy and Xing Han Lu initially favored the browser approach but later moved toward the tool-based one, since agents struggled with graphical interfaces. Plug-ins such as Gmail and Instacart connectors already let agents perform tasks by using text commands behind the scenes. Muse, for example, can make purchases through a Stripe Link connector, but the agent never sees the card number and a human must confirm each purchase.

Progress has been rapid. OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, released last September, achieved a 73% success rate on OSWorld 2.0, a benchmark for complex multistep computer tasks. Ethan Mollick of the Wharton School said the agentic web "is here earlier than people expected."

Not everyone welcomes this shift. Soon after Meta released Muse in September, Amazon blocked it from its site, saying it had not authorized access and that Muse undermines its ability to personalize shopping. The article notes that Amazon has its own shopping agent, Alexa for Shopping. Agents could also threaten the advertising-based business model of the web, since fewer people click through to websites. A Pew study found people were about 40% less likely to click through from Google results when an AI summary appeared, and one analysis found some publisher ad revenue fell by about a third between 2025 and 2026. E-commerce sites are also uncertain how to adapt, since a study by Akshit Kumar's team found agents were less likely to recommend items tagged as sponsored, though their preferences for results positions varied across models.

Some experts see possible benefits. Microsoft economist David Rothschild suggested agents could make micropayments for individual articles or videos practical, while Wellesley professor Eni Mustafaraj hopes agents could reshape feeds around users' wishes rather than platforms'. Ajit Varma of Mozilla imagined agents that could deal directly with restaurants and bypass service fees. But the article warns that web history has tended toward consolidation, and companies such as Meta might design their agents to keep users inside their own platforms. OpenAI bought OpenClaw's creator, Peter Steinberger, after the grassroots assistant agent appeared in early 2026. Closed systems also have safety advantages, such as blocking hacking-related requests, though Rothschild noted they can mean less growth and less equitable growth.

The article compares this shift to the arrival of the iPhone in 2007 and the App Store in 2008, which changed the web without replacing it and left some businesses and media behind. Rothschild expects similar losses and new businesses that cannot yet be imagined. People who avoid agents could be cut off from some services, as happened with apps such as Signal, Hinge, and WeChat, and with the CBP One tool. Agents could also help elderly and disabled people who struggle with conventional interfaces, according to Margaret Mitchell of Hugging Face. Opera executive Krystian Kolondra said he would use agents for routine tasks such as finding flights but would still plan fun trips himself. Mollick worried that if agents take over the web, the human internet could fade, and he said that "we have no idea" how things will develop.

incogni.note: Total privacy-risk score = 'AI and user data' + 'Transparency' + 'Data collection and sharing' from Incogni's published chart data (lower = less privacy-invasive). 13 platforms scored.

obscureiq.name: ObscureIQ: Which Generative AI Is Most Privacy-Respecting? (2025 edition)
obscureiq.note: Privacy posture score out of 5 (higher = more private), weighted: prompt retention 25%, training opt-out 20%, jurisdiction 15%, transparency 15%, user control 15%, default behavior 10%. By Jeff Jockisch; page says 'Last verified October 2025'. Page opened and scores read on 2026-11-07.

privacy.how: Average of 2 independent privacy rankings: Incogni 2026 and ObscureIQ.
privacy.checksNote: The checks under each app are information from the companies' own pages; they don't count in the score.

rule: A model is called best when at least 3 of the tests for its task put it in their top 3 (all 3 when a task has only 3). Pictures have only 1 source, so no picture model is called best.
